Restless Development India  is putting young people in charge of mental health and queer-affirmative change in Dakshinpuri, Delhi.

QUTWE : Queer-affirmative Unicorns Transforming Wellbeing Ecosystem

Young people turned silence into community.

In Dakshinpuri, Delhi, trained young people built a mental health and queer-affirmative support ecosystem with one central aim: bringing parents and their children closer together. In 18 months, stigma fell, resilience nearly doubled, and over 700 youth and parents were reached.

The innovation at the heart of it all

One youth-run safe space, at the centre of everything.

The Youth Resource Centre is a youth-led, community-embedded, non-judgemental safe space in Dakshinpuri. Peer support, family dialogue, and affirmative care all run through it, working toward one goal: parents and children who understand and accept each other.

How it all works together

Every stage of the cycle builds toward one central aim: stronger connectedness between young people and their parents.

Foundation · Months 1–4
Building trust before building systems.
Community mapping, establishment of the Youth Resource Centre, and recruitment of 10 Youth Unicorns and 12 Parent Role Models. The YRC was designed to be safe and non-clinical — a space to arrive in before anything was asked of anyone.
10 Youth Unicorns + 12 Parent Role Models
Capacity Building · Months 3–7
Youth Unicorns become community mental health leaders.
A 6-month-long PFA training and supervision programme by expert facilitators — covering trauma-informed facilitation, grief, suicide prevention, and mental health literacy. Youth Unicorns were not just trained — they were prepared to hold space for others.
6-month PFA programme · certified by IAmWellbeing
Delivery · Months 5–15
40 Wellbeing Circles. 500+ young people in workshops.
40 Wellbeing Circles reaching 383 young people with peer-led discussion on identity, grief, family, and mental health. Interactive Workshops co-designed by Youth Unicorns reached 500+ young people, covering SOGIESC, emotional regulation, and help-seeking.
383 young people · 500+ in workshops
One-to-One Support · Months 5–18
250+ individual psychosocial support interactions.
Recognising different support needs, Youth Unicorns provided 250+ one-to-one psychosocial support interactions — emotional support, distress identification, and facilitated referrals to queer-affirmative mental health professionals.
250+ PFA interactions
Family Engagement · Months 6–16
183 parents engaged. Parents become allies, not bystanders.
12 Parent Role Models mobilised caregivers through community conversations — reducing stigma and opening doors to identity conversations. Months of trust-building before any joint dialogues began.
183 parents reached
Intergenerational · Months 12–17
Parents and young people in the same room.
6 intergenerational dialogues brought 36 young people and 36 parents together in facilitated conversations — practising active listening, empathy, and open communication. 60+ participants in open dialogues at the YRC during International Days of Family.
72 participants · 6 dialogues
Ecosystem · Months 8–18
A referral network, shared commitments, and a new tool.
Referral pathways formalised with 11 queer-affirmative providers. 45 practitioners signed the Statement of Shared Commitments. The PYCS — the first validated connectedness scale for LGBTQIA+ youth in India — developed and validated (Cronbach's alpha 0.92).
11 providers · 45 commitments · PYCS α = 0.92

01

The Challenge

Mental health was unspoken, queer youth were unseen, and there was no public psychiatric facility within 5km of Dakshinpuri.

+9%increase in resilience (ARM-R)
Read more →
i.

Young people had no language for their own minds.

Distress went unnamed and unmet. Mental health was understood as weakness, and few young people knew how to recognise it or seek help.

ii.

At the root: fractured parent-youth relationships.

The deepest driver of distress was disconnection at home. Stigma around identity (SOGIESC) left parents without the language to accept their children, and for many queer young people, home was the least safe place to be known.

iii.

Services were neither youth-friendly nor queer-affirmative.

Where mental health support existed, it was often stigmatising. At the start of the programme, there was no public psychiatric facility within 5 kilometres of Dakshinpuri. LGBTQIA+ youth faced rejection at the very doors meant to help them.

06

Family Connectedness

The central aim of the whole programme. Connectedness has begun to rise, measured by the only validated parent-child tool built for queer youth in this context (alpha 0.92).

0.92scale reliability score
Read more →

Building stronger families from the inside out.

Changing what happens between a parent and child at home is slow, relational work. QUTWE invested in it seriously: training parents as community role models, opening intergenerational dialogue, and building the only measurement tool designed for this community's reality.

We did not just measure it. We built the only tool designed to measure it in this context.

No validated scale existed that centred queer and trans youth experiences in low-income urban India. So we built one from scratch. The PYCS went through ethics approval, FGDs with 54 community members, three expert reviews, and a pilot with 120 young people before it reached the field.

Development process
✔ Ethics approval received
✔ FGDs: 37 youth + 17 parents
✔ 125-item pool generated
✔ Expert review: 3 specialists
✔ Pilot: 120 young people
✔ Final: 35 items, 3 domains
Scale reliability
0.92 alpha
Cronbach's alpha on the final 35-item scale, indicating high internal reliability.
What this means

A score of 0.92 means the scale's 35 questions consistently measure the same thing. In plain terms: the tool is reliable, and the results can be trusted.

What the scale found: three domains
Domain A

Emotional Attachment and Support

Closeness, care, emotional availability, and ability to share distress with parents.

What the pilot showed

Young people care deeply for their parents while not feeling able to turn to them for emotional support.

Domain B

Autonomy, Control and Acceptance

Decision-making, trust, parental control, and acceptance of choices around appearance, friendships, and relationships.

What the pilot showed

Parental involvement in life decisions coexists with experiences of scolding, control, and social reputation concerns.

Domain C

Support for Perceived LGBTQIA+ Identity

How young people expect parents would respond if they came out: willingness to listen, accept, protect, and advocate. Framed around perceived response because fear shapes behaviour even before disclosure happens.

What the pilot showed

The lowest perceived safety across the scale. Yet some items showed cautious hope: uncertainty rather than absolute rejection, pointing to real entry points for dialogue.

08

Key Insights

Mental health literacy and resilience moved most, family connectedness is on the move and needs sustained investment, and the 6-month PFA design proved essential.

4key learnings from 18 months
Read more →
What worked

A youth-run space made youth-led change possible.

The biggest shifts came where young people led from their own Resource Centre. Peer-to-peer trust opened doors that outside services could not. Capacity cannot be rushed: the 6-month PFA design was essential.

What surprised us

Acceptance moved fastest of all.

We expected knowledge to climb. We did not expect attitudes toward supporting a peer in distress to rise 31%, the most of any outcome measured.

What we invested in deeply

Family change is relational and takes time.

Connectedness and affirmation at home moved steadily. Building the PYCS, training 12 Parent Role Models, and opening intergenerational dialogue are investments that compound in the next phase.

What we learned

Family change is slower — and moving in the right direction.

Parent-reported affective responsiveness improved significantly (d=0.33). Intergenerational dialogues began only in month 12, giving family outcomes the shortest window to mature. A longer programme period is the evidence-based lever for converting direction into significance.

09

Looking Forward

Proven in one community. The Youth Resource Centre model is replicable, the cadre is trained, the scale is validated. Ready for more.

3priorities for the next phase
Read more →

QUTWE was designed as a proof of concept: a test of whether one youth-run safe space could shift mental health, stigma, and family acceptance in a low-resource community. The test returned a clear yes, and a model ready to scale across similar settings in India.

Priority 01

Replicate the Resource Centre model in new communities.

The proof of concept holds. A youth-run safe space is replicable, locally owned, and cost-effective.

Evidence: +16% mental health literacy, +9% resilience, +20% service confidence
Priority 02

Deepen and lengthen family work.

Connectedness moved least. The next investment belongs in sustained intergenerational engagement with families.

Evidence: family shift +4%, the slowest
Priority 03

Sustain and grow the Youth Unicorn cadre.

These trained young leaders are the engine of the model. Retaining and growing them is how impact compounds.

Evidence: 22 trained leaders, 700+ reached

A model that is ready to travel.

QUTWE started as one question: can a youth-run safe space shift mental health, stigma, and family acceptance in a low-resource community? After 18 months in Dakshinpuri, the answer is yes. The Youth Resource Centre model is replicable. The Youth Unicorn cadre is trained. The Parent-Youth Connectedness Scale is validated and field-tested. The referral network is live. Everything needed to take this to the next community already exists.

Evidence & Methodology

Validated instruments, real sample sizes, transparent reporting. All effect sizes, sample sizes, and scale notes in one place.

5validated instruments, 700+ participants
Read more →

Every claim above rests on validated psychometric instruments and real sample sizes. We are transparent about method and about one issue we caught and corrected.

What we measuredInstrumentnBaselineEndlineShiftEffect size
Mental health literacy (overall)MHLS5102.783.23+16%d = 1.43
Confidence in services & resourcesMHLS (Q18+Q19)5102.933.52+20%d = 0.54
ResilienceARM-R5062.973.24+9%d = 0.49
ResilienceARM-R5062.973.24+9%d = 0.49
Which analysis is this? All figures on this page come from the full-sample group-level analysis (507 baseline respondents vs 510 endline respondents, independent samples, Welch's t-test). This is the primary and most defensible figure — the full cohort, not just those we could individually trace. Baseline and endline were independent samples (repeated cross-section), so shifts describe community-level change, not within-person tracking.
We also ran two further analyses to cross-check: (1) Matched individual pairs — 263 youth individually paired across waves by name and age (51.6% match rate); (2) Unmatched group comparison — the ~247 endline-only respondents vs ~244 baseline-only respondents who could not be individually traced. All three analyses tell the same story: MHLS and ARM-R improvements are significant and consistent; PYCS and FAD overall are flat or improving. Full details are in the Evidence tab.
Effect size guide. Cohen's d: >0.8 large · 0.5 medium · 0.2 small. FAD runs higher = less healthy (McMaster convention), so a falling FAD score is an improvement.
FAD note. The Family Assessment Device runs higher = less healthy functioning (McMaster convention). Improvements show as a falling score. Item 31 was not collected in either wave.

Custom PYCS. The Parent-Youth Connectedness Scale was developed by Restless Development India: 3-phase mixed-methods process, FGDs with 37 youth and 17 parents, piloted with 120 participants, final 35 items, Cronbach's alpha 0.92.

The Theory of Change

COM-B: how behaviour change actually works

QUTWE's four outcomes sit on a single logic: Capability (literacy) must precede Motivation (resilience), which creates the conditions for Opportunity (family communication). Outcomes requiring longer sustained exposure — PYCS, FAD overall — are consistent with implementation science evidence on relational, dyadic change.

Transition to Scale

Ready to scale.
Ready to go further.

The proof of concept holds. The model is peer-led, locally owned, evidence-backed — and designed from day one to be replicable beyond Dakshinpuri.

Why This Model Is Ready

Three things make QUTWE different.

01 · Evidence
Three independent analyses. Same story.
MHLS (+16%, d=1.43) and ARM-R (+9%, d=0.49) are significant across matched, unmatched, and full-sample analyses. GCC's Transition-to-Scale phase requires evidence that survives multiple analytical tests — this does.
02 · Replicability
A curriculum, not a person. A space, not a project.
Youth Unicorns are trained to a structured, documented curriculum. The PFA programme, supervision model, Wellbeing Circle facilitation guide, and PYCS measurement tool all exist as transferable assets — ready to stand up in any urban informal settlement.
03 · The Theory Predicts It
Relational outcomes need more time. The model knows this.
COM-B and implementation science (Durlak & DuPre, 2008) both predict that family-level and dyadic outcomes lag individual ones. PYCS and FAD are moving the right way. A longer window converts direction into significance — which is exactly what the scale phase provides.

Beyond the Numbers

A community ecosystem that outlasts the project.

A referral network, a validated measurement tool, 45 practitioners who signed shared commitments, and an ongoing research partnership continuing beyond the project period.

Statement of Shared Commitments

45 practitioners and organisations endorsed seven core principles — psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, counselling psychologists, psychotherapists, hospital-based practitioners, and mental health collectives, including Naz Foundation, Qafila, I Am Wellbeing, Dr Sohini Banerjee, Dinika Anand, and Bhanu Kharbanda.

  • →Every young person deserves safe, respectful, confidential mental health services regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.
  • →Services must be queer-affirming, youth-friendly, and responsive to socioeconomic realities.
  • →Affordability is essential; financial and structural barriers must be reduced.
  • →Parent–youth connection should be recognised as protective when safe and youth-led.
  • →Young people's autonomy, confidentiality, and informed consent remain central.
  • →Cross-sector collaboration strengthens care pathways.
  • →Continuous learning and evidence-informed practice are essential for inclusive, affirmative mental health services.

Referral Network — Expanding Access to Affirmative Mental Health Support

11 public and private providers joined the referral network, offering a range of support options from pro bono and sliding-scale services to paid care — including Naz Foundation (India) Trust, Qafila: Psychosocial Support & Research, I Am Wellbeing (Nairatmya Foundation), and independent queer-affirmative practitioners. This gave young people access to a diverse, trusted ecosystem of mental health support directly from the Youth Resource Centre.

The PYCS Tool — A Contribution to the Field

The Parent–Youth Connectedness Scale (PYCS) is a validated 35-item instrument measuring connectedness for LGBTQIA+ young people in India — the first of its kind. Developed through FGDs with 37 youth and 17 parents, expert review, and piloting with 120 respondents. Cronbach's alpha: 0.92. The scale has since been presented at national and international platforms as a field contribution beyond the QUTWE programme.

Influencing the Mental Health Ecosystem Beyond QUTWE

Over the course of implementation, QUTWE evolved from a community intervention into a recognised model shaping wider conversations on youth mental health, LGBTQIA+ inclusion, and family-centred approaches.

National Platforms
  • Manotsava National Mental Health Festival — Restless Development, CMHLP, and Sangath hosted a lived-experience stall on QUTWE and Youth Unicorns. First public introduction of PYCS. Dr Souvik joined a panel on queer mental health.
  • QUTWE Learning Convening, Delhi (Feb 2026) — Restless Development convened practitioners, researchers, youth advocates, donors, and partners to reflect on programme learning and gather practitioner feedback on PYCS.
International Platforms
  • Bold Ideas for Brighter Futures 2026 (2nd Global Conference on Child & Adolescent Mental Health, Cape Town) — PYCS presented to a global audience.
  • IAYMT Conference 2026, Dublin — Abstract accepted on strengthening parent–youth connectedness among marginalised queer young people in Delhi.
  • Violence Ends With Us Asia-Pacific Summit, Manila — Samar Sharma represented QUTWE on a regional panel on marginalised and at-risk communities.
Emerging Partnerships
UNICEF (MHPSS team + India Country Office) · CMHLP (learning from the Atmiyata model) · Hasiru Dala Innovations (integrating climate change, children's mental health, and parent–youth connectedness)

Beyond QUTWE: Advancing Community Mental Health Research in Dakshinpuri

As QUTWE concludes (June 2026), Restless Development and I Am Wellbeing have launched an ongoing research partnership building on the trust established through QUTWE. The first study examines Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) in the Indian context, capturing adversities standard ACE frameworks miss — housing insecurity, displacement, discrimination, educational pressure, and socio-cultural restrictions.

Preliminary Findings (n=168)
35.7%
witnessed neighbourhood violence
30.3%
experienced discrimination or unfair treatment
25.4%
witnessed violence between caregivers
25%
experienced food insecurity
25%
experienced homelessness or displacement
18.9%
experienced sexual abuse

The research continues beyond the project period. Findings will inform future programme design and both partners intend to use the evidence to engage funders for the next phase of mental health programming in Dakshinpuri.

Voices from Dakshinpuri

Stories of change.

These are not case studies. They are accounts of what it meant for young people — and their families — to be seen, heard, and supported for the first time.

A
Ananya she/her
19 yrs  ·  Youth participant
01
"For the first time, I could say out loud what I was feeling. The Wellbeing Circle gave me the words."

Ananya came to the YRC after a friend told her about the Wellbeing Circles. She had never spoken about her mental health to anyone. Over six months she found a vocabulary for her own distress and, eventually, the confidence to have a conversation with her mother about her identity. She now co-facilitates a Circle herself.

R
Rohan he/him
22 yrs  ·  Youth Unicorn
02
"I always thought asking for help meant I was weak. QUTWE showed me it takes more strength."

Rohan was one of the first Youth Unicorns recruited. Initially sceptical about the PFA training, he found that learning to hold space for others changed how he held space for himself. He went on to lead outreach in his neighbourhood, reaching young men who would otherwise never have engaged with a mental health programme.

P
Priya she/her
17 yrs  ·  Youth participant
03
"My mother didn't understand at first. After the dialogue session, something shifted between us."

Priya joined as one of the youngest participants. Her relationship with her mother was strained — identity, expectation, and silence had built a wall between them. After attending an Intergenerational Dialogue together, they began talking again. Her mother became a Parent Role Model the following year.

K
Kamla she/her
42 yrs  ·  Parent Role Model
04
"I thought I knew my daughter. The dialogue made me realise I had been hearing but not listening."

Kamla joined as a Parent Role Model after her daughter encouraged her to attend a YRC event. Over months of conversations with other parents and a Youth Unicorn, she began to understand what her daughter had been carrying alone. She now runs informal conversations with mothers in her building.

S
Siddharth they/them
21 yrs  ·  Youth Unicorn
05
"There was nowhere in Dakshinpuri that felt safe to be myself. The YRC changed that."

Siddharth grew up hiding every part of their identity. When they first walked into the YRC, they sat in the back and said nothing. By month four, they were leading a Wellbeing Circle on SOGIESC. Their MHLS score was one of the largest individual gains in the matched dataset. They are now exploring a career in counselling.

M
Meera she/her
25 yrs  ·  Youth Unicorn
06
"I trained as a Youth Unicorn to help others. I didn't expect it to help me this much."

Meera had experienced her own mental health crisis two years before joining the programme. As a Youth Unicorn, she provided over 30 one-to-one psychosocial support interactions — more than any other Unicorn in the cohort. She has since enrolled in a part-time counselling psychology programme.

Names have been changed to protect participant privacy. Stories are composites informed by participant feedback collected during Wellbeing Circles and one-to-one support interactions.
